content: Caregivers should identify the specific site on the body where an injectable vaccine was administered or simulate the act of administering oral drops to inquire about oral polio or rotavirus vaccines. It is important to ask when the vaccine was received in relation to other documented vaccinations. When discussing this, it is recommended to use visual aids that align with national vaccination practices to facilitate understanding. A child may have been vaccinated at a health center that is not the one closest to their residence. In such cases, it may not be possible to locate the vaccination record at the nearest health center. This highlights the importance of accurate documentation and communication between health facilities. These tools include templates and examples for reporting and visualizing data, which are intended to serve as a starting point for users. For example, data on vaccine acceptance intentions can be analyzed across demographic characteristics such as gender, age, education level, and employment type. Statistical methods, such as univariate and multivariate logistic regression models, can be used to assess associations between vaccine intentions and demographic variables. The guidance emphasizes the use of human-centered design to tailor immunization programs. This involves investigating the drivers of vaccination behavior, such as trust in healthcare workers, support from religious leaders, and recommendations from health professionals. Data visualization tools can be used to represent findings, such as the percentage of individuals who heard negative information about vaccines or those who trust healthcare workers. When reporting findings, users are encouraged to provide detailed descriptions of the research methods, including sampling approaches, recruitment methods, data handling, and ethical considerations. The findings should be presented in a way that highlights key themes and concepts, supported by quotes or examples where applicable. The guidance also outlines steps for implementing interventions based on findings. This includes describing the intervention, the stakeholders involved, and the partnerships or resources available to support implementation. Monitoring and evaluation plans should be developed to track progress and assess the impact of the intervention. Key successes and challenges during implementation should be documented, along with lessons learned and recommendations for scaling up or replicating the intervention. Finally, the guidance includes a policy on data sharing and use, emphasizing the importance of ethical and secure handling of data. Data provided to the World Health Organization (WHO) must comply with national laws, including data protection regulations. WHO may publish and analyze de-identified data for public health purposes, ensuring acknowledgment of the contributing country.
